stories.headline: Trump Reaffirms Deportation Stance Amid Poll Support
stories.hook: At a White House briefing, President Trump stood firm with charts showing public backing for deportations, pushing back against amnesty ideas from reporters.
stories.summary: Trump rejected broad legal status for 20 to 30 million illegal immigrants, declaring 'WE’RE NOT gonna let immigration destroy our country' while noting Hispanic support for deportations and border security. A new YouGov poll found 51 percent of Americans favor deporting most illegal immigrants, with only 7 percent wanting all to stay, though older surveys show support for limited paths for long-term residents. Officials like JD Vance criticized amnesty calls, and the administration appointed Stephen Miller as chief of staff, signaling focus on criminals and border enforcement despite some flexibility on DACA.

stories.headline: Senate Republicans Re-Elect Thune as Leader After Midterm Losses
stories.hook: One week after losing the Senate majority, Republicans rallied behind John Thune in a closed-door vote, but online critics erupted with fury over his past leadership.
stories.summary: On November 10, South Dakota Senator John Thune won re-election as GOP Senate leader by acclamation, facing no challengers despite the party's midterm defeat. Conservative voices online lashed out, calling him a failure, traitor, or RINO for perceived shortcomings in advancing Trump-era priorities like the SAVE America Act. While Thune's colleagues valued his stability and President Trump once called him a good man, the decision highlighted deep rifts between Senate Republicans and their frustrated base.

stories.headline: Satirical Tweet Imagines Trump Backing Medicare for All as Jeffries Says No
stories.hook: A cheeky tweet pictures a wild twist: Trump ready to pass Medicare for All, only for Hakeem Jeffries to block it. The idea hit a nerve amid fresh midterm shifts.
stories.summary: The post by @ostonox, racking up tens of thousands of likes, pokes at Trump's recent talk of 'great healthcare' teamwork with Democrats, who now control Congress from January 2026. Jeffries favors smaller steps like lowering Medicare's age and adding dental coverage, but not full single-payer that scraps most private insurance. Critics like Neera Tanden dismissed it as another Trump feint, citing his ACA repeal efforts, while others saw it as satire spotlighting left-wing strategy debates. Experts note big reforms face vetoes and filibusters, with incremental changes gaining traction.

stories.headline: Obama Urges Democratic Freshmen to Embrace Diversity and Push Health Care Reforms
stories.hook: In a closed-door pep talk, Barack Obama painted a vivid picture of the House chamber: one side like a uniform golf country club, the other reflecting all of America.
stories.summary: Speaking to incoming House Democratic freshmen in Washington this week, former President Obama praised the new class's diversity and urged them to bridge internal differences while delivering for constituents. He contrasted the House sides during his State of the Union addresses, drawing laughter but sparking online backlash where critics called the 'country club' remark divisive and highlighted his own golf club ties. Obama also advised pushing beyond Affordable Care Act fixes toward bolder health reforms like public options, a move energizing some progressives as Democrats gear up for the new Congress.

stories.headline: Trump's Immigration Remarks Divide His Supporters
stories.hook: At a White House press conference, Trump floated possible deals with Democrats on immigration relief, while VP Vance and Secretary Rubio stood by looking uneasy.
stories.summary: Trump suggested cooperation with Democrats on issues involving long-term illegal immigrants, sparking backlash from his base who see it as straying from strict enforcement promises. Conservative voices like Tomi Lahren warned against trusting Democrats on border security, amid a YouGov poll showing 51% of Americans favor deporting most illegal immigrants with few exceptions. Some defend the comments as strategic maneuvering to secure concessions, while others insist Trump never endorsed amnesty and prioritizes criminal removals first. The split highlights tensions as Trump navigates post-midterm priorities like border security and bipartisan options.

stories.headline: Americans Split on Affordability Crisis Amid Rising Inflation
stories.hook: Only 17% of adults believe today's children will have it better than their parents, capturing deep economic unease across the board.
stories.summary: President Trump blames high prices on the prior Biden administration, claiming they are now way down, while supporters argue an information operation misled voters on affordability. Critics point to Trump's tariffs and the ongoing Iran conflict, which spiked energy prices with gasoline up 9.1% in September as inflation hit 3.7%. A post-election survey showed voters more likely to blame tariffs than the war itself, reflecting divided views on groceries, energy, and housing costs.

stories.headline: Debate Intensifies Over Trump's Affordability Crisis Claims
stories.hook: Two years into Donald Trump's second term, polls show only 17% of Americans believe kids will have it better than their parents—a stark sign of economic unease.
stories.summary: Social media users fiercely debate whether high costs for gas, groceries, and housing stem from Trump policies like tariffs or lingering Biden-era inflation. Trump counters that his administration inherited the problem and has lowered prices through tax cuts and energy boosts, while critics blame him for ongoing 3.7% inflation above Fed targets. Midterm losses handed Democrats House and Senate control, driven by voter frustration over living costs as the top issue.

stories.headline: GOP Tensions Rise as Congress Nears End with Johnson Urging Attendance
stories.hook: With just 44 days left before Democrats take the Senate majority, Speaker Mike Johnson is calling every Republican back to Washington—except for serious medical issues—to push through key bills.
stories.summary: Johnson's November 20 letter highlights the House passing over 1,000 measures while Senate Democrats blocked nearly 700, stressing the need to advance government funding, the NDAA, and more before January. Conservatives are voicing frustration at Senate Majority Leader John Thune, with President Trump blaming him for stalling military funding and air traffic control reforms, and a White House official citing a held-up $350 billion Pentagon boost. Meanwhile, Rep. Tim Burchett announced his 2028 Senate run in Tennessee, polling strongly and drawing cheers as a conservative fighter. These moves underscore Republican pressure to act aggressively in their final weeks of unified control.
